title: Liking is not learning
statement: Don't read liking as learning: in one study every kind of picture raised satisfaction, but only instructive ones raised recall.
detail:
In a published study, every kind of graphic raised satisfaction ratings over no graphics, but only the instructive
graphics raised recall (Sung & Mayer 2012, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2012.03.026). No student has used any version
of my film (`g9/README.md`), so how much anyone liked it says nothing yet about what it teaches.
against:
liking still
matters for whether anyone watches at all, and nothing here measures that. A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/skills/reading-science/DIGEST-rand-mr1465-2002.qmd`).

evidence.quote: AI presenters show no reliable learning loss, but a real engagement and comfort loss
interest tested flat as a learning driver, so it was struck from the record (Honesty log).
restudy feels productive, but retrieval produces stronger delayed learning.
Warns us not to rely on students’ subjective ease or fluency as indicators of mastery
“Looks more animated” alone is not evidence of better teaching.
A visual preference alone cannot establish comprehension gains.
If an app performs well on engagement but poorly on externally validated outcomes, the closed loop forces the conversation back to instruction, mastery, and signal integrity.
"the most predictive statistical models show that engagement is a mediator of the effects of instruction on reading achievement"
A generator optimizing for pass-rates or engagement will quietly lower rigor
**No significant difference in academic performance** between AI and human instructor conditions. **Video engagement was higher with the human instructor.**

evidence.quote: A video that is enjoyed and teaches nothing has not done the job.

evidence.path: BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md
evidence.quote: Accepted as evidence, refused as advice. Enjoyment is not the reading, SPOV1
**A generator optimizing for pass-rates or engagement will quietly lower rigor and destroy the very thing that works.**
That is encouragement, not acceptance, certification, or proof of learning.
A claim that learners achieved an objective should be supported by an observable student action that demonstrates that objective; task completion or engagement alone does not establish it.
An engaging performance without intellectual follow-through is insufficient.
